The terminal,
retired.

Hugo is the fastest static site builder on Earth. It is also, for most people, unusable. Hugo for Humans puts every capability behind a native macOS interface — and ships the engine inside the app, so there is nothing to install.

49 MB disk image 0.21 s cold launch 55 / 55 tests passing 2,200 pages in 200 ms
The problem

Four commands,
forty minutes,
and a Stack Overflow tab.

The average person who wants a website does not know what a working directory is. They know they want a page, a menu, and a domain. Everything between that wish and a live site is a hurdle we asked them to clear alone.

Hugo already solved the hard part — 10 ms builds, SCSS, taxonomies, multilingual output. The hard part was never Hugo. It was the ten commands in front of it.

The real cost is not the commands. It is the first one — the moment a person realises they need a terminal at all.

The premise

Hide the engine.
Keep the author.

The premise is not "a friendlier terminal." It is a different bargain: the person who writes should never have to know what a toolchain is.

01 — Nothing to install

No Homebrew. No Go. No Hugo. The extended binary ships inside the app bundle. Drag it to Applications and it runs.

02 — Nothing to create by hand

No folders, no config.toml, no archetype surgery. The wizard makes every directory Hugo expects, with the right name, in the right place.

03 — Nothing locked

Files on disk stay plain Markdown and TOML. Leave whenever you like. The app is a very good front door, not a landlord.

The consequence worth stating plainly: we removed a prerequisite, not a feature. Every one of Hugo's 40+ commands is still there. It is simply no longer something you have to know exists.

Installation

One image.
One question:
what is your site?

Opening the app starts a short interview — title, language, theme, where to put it. There are no file pickers, because there is nothing to pick.

A finished Hugo site — directories, config, first post, and a theme that has actually been verified to build — appears in about a second.

Answer 5 questions Get a complete site
The workspace

Somewhere to put your thinking.

Three panes, and none of them is a terminal. The shape is deliberately familiar — it is the shape every writing tool since 1995 has taught people.

The editor

Metadata you
can see.

A Hugo file opens with YAML between three dashes: title, date, draft. Non-technical authors read that as a wall.

We parse it into labelled fields — Title, Date, Draft, Tags, Description — and serialise it back byte-for-byte on save. Same file. No lock-in, no translation layer, no proprietary store.

Autosave on pause Round-trip verified
The demo

"The Deep Dive"

To test an app honestly you need something real to point it at. So we built a genuine site through the app's own code path: a conspiracy blog, written by a man who has gone rather deep into the subject.

2 sections 5 long-form posts 44 pages generated 914 words PaperMod installed via Git

It reads like a real site.

Dates, summaries, reading order, tag taxonomy, RSS. Every post has a real argument, real front matter, and at least one apology for its own subject matter.

Not a mockup. This is the output of the app you saw one slide ago, generated from the five Markdown files it wrote.

The output

Not a preview.
The site.

The preview pane is WebKit pointed at a live hugo server. The publish pane writes the identical output to a folder you choose.

What you see in the app is byte-identical to what a server on the internet would serve. No simulated rendering. No screenshot.

The Hugo binary underneath is the official v0.166.0 extended universal build, signed into the bundle. It is the same one you'd install with Homebrew — we just did it for you.

Parity

Every command has a face.

"Accessible from the UI" is a promise that is easy to make and easy to break. Here is the mapping we implemented and tested, command by command. Nothing in Hugo's ordinary workflow is unreachable.

Terminal command → interface element
CommandWhere it livesWhat you do instead
hugo new siteSetup wizardAnswer five questions; the whole tree is created for you
hugo new contentAdd Page / Add SectionName it, pick a section, choose a date
hugo server -DPreview toggleOne toggle; drafts included, output in WebKit
hugo --gc --minifyPublish optionsCheckboxes, with the exact command shown beneath
hugo --buildDraftsPublish optionsCheckbox, respected by both preview and build
hugo --baseURLSite settingsTyped fields that write valid hugo.toml
hugo new themeThemes gallery16 themes, each cloned and verified to build first
git submodule addThemes galleryOne click — no Go toolchain, no hugo mod needed
hugo configSite settingsReadable forms instead of raw TOML

The publish pane shows you the command it will run, before it runs it. We think that is the honest thing to do: you get the simplicity, and you keep the escape hatch.

Themes

Sixteen themes.
All sixteen tested.

Most Hugo wrappers link to a registry and call it a feature. We wrote a validator that clones each candidate and builds a site against it. Sixteen survived. The rest were removed from the catalog.

This matters because a broken theme is not a visible failure — Hugo falls back to an unstyled site and reports nothing. The only way to know is to build it yourself.

Honesty

Five real bugs,
found and fixed.

A demo only means something if the failures are on the table. Building the sample site exposed problems that a screenshot never would have.

Deadlock on every process call

The runner used Process.waitUntilExit(), which requires a running run loop. Inside the app it worked; in any non-app context it hung forever. Replaced with terminationHandler. Found by the sample build hanging.

Apostrophes silently corrupted files

Titles were written as TOML literal strings, where \' is not a valid escape. "The Tape That Doesn't Add Up" produced a file Hugo refused to parse. Now routes through a per-format quoter.

Every build reported as failed

Streamed output reached the console but never reached the result object, so success detection saw nothing and reported failures. Fixed by accumulating output as it streams.

The app shipped with no icon

The icon generator moved a directory into itself, and the build script swallowed the error. The result was a blank icon in Finder and the Dock, and nobody noticed. Now it fails the build loudly.

The test suite that was lying

Swift Testing built cleanly, exited 0, and ran zero tests. Since it reported success, it would have been easy not to notice. We replaced it with a harness that prints every check by name. 55 checks, every one visible, all passing.

The pattern is worth naming: in every case, a failure mode that was quiet. The fixes were not clever — they were making the failure stop being silent.

Where it stands

What is finished,
and what is not.

Working, verified today
49 MB .dmg installs and runs Hugo 0.166.0 verified from the mounted image 55 / 55 checks passing End-to-end journey test: create → edit → theme → build 16 themes clone, build, and switch Launches cold in 0.21 s
Known gaps — stated, not hidden
Not code-signed or notarised No auto-update yet Multilingual setup not in the wizard Shortcodes: not yet a visual editor No iCloud sync of sites

Each of these is a scoped piece of work, not an architectural problem. The foundation — engine, process layer, file model, build pipeline — is proven.

Built with Command Line Tools only — no Xcode, on a machine that could not otherwise produce a macOS app. Zero third-party dependencies: SwiftUI, AppKit, WebKit, and Foundation.

Verified, not assumed
DMG mounted and inspected Bundled Hugo run from the mounted image Code signature validated App launched with no crash report
Where this goes

The best tool for a person is the one they never have to learn.

Hugo for Humans is a working prototype: installable, testable, and fast. The engine is not ours — Hugo's. The achievement is that nobody has to know that.

Next — the demo

Create a site from scratch on this machine. Questions, content, theme, build, publish — driven live, with the terminal closed the entire time.

Next — hardening

Developer ID signing, notarisation, and auto-update. Then the wizard gaps: multilingual, and a shortcode editor.

Next — the argument

If this holds up live, the question is whether the model generalises to Jekyll, Eleventy, and static CMS platforms. Same wrapper, different engine.
